Father a Nation

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
At a time where South Africa is going through a masculinity crises Father a Nation has pledged to make men that women and children can be proud of

Unique Selling Point:
Father A Nation
Broken people breed broken families and broken families breed broken communities that breed broken nations.
This statement is so relevant in a country like South Africa where fatherlessness on a massive scale is the consequence of our history of migrant labour and apartheid. In a country where 18673 people were murdered and there were 51895 reported cases of gender based violence in 2016 alone.

Father A Nation is a program that is aimed at trying to offer a solution to this masculinity crises taking place in South Africa
Currently the program is being run in De Aar. 50 men went on 5 weekend camps to rehabilitate them into being fathers to the boys who have lost their way within the community.

The program was the brainchild of Craig Wilkinson. After his wife and children where hijacked and his wife was shot in the face he moved his family to Knysna. It was here he started getting involved in community development and Father A Nation was born

From the 50 men that just went through the program we will tell the story of
Character 1: Francis Jonker
Character 2: Sam Plaaitjies

Each man will take us with them on a mentoring session with a young boy. Both boys have been in hangs and both have been abandoned by their fathers. They may want to remain anonymous.

We will also see all 50 men graduate and make their pledge to being better men.

Craig is extremely articulate and educated on the impact of fatherlessness on South Africa. He has worked with various international universities on studies on the issue.




Further information:
Some scary stats about Fatherlessness in SA

9 million children grow up without fathers in South Africa,
63% of youth suicides are from fatherless homes;
More than a third of the country’s prisoners are aged 18 – 25.
Nearly 50 000 school girls became pregnant in 2007 a 151% increase since 2003.
Nearly a third of 12 – 14 year olds said they had easy access to marijuana and 8% had easy access to crack cocaine.

Press Release:


Father a Nation
Does growing up without a father, make young men more susceptible to negative influences? Researchers believe that broken people breed broken families
and in turn, broken communities. But a new programme aims to address South Africa’s masculinity crisis.

Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
00:00 Father a Nation
Man 1: As a man amongst men I'm a man,
Man 2: As a man amongst men I'm a knowledgeable man.
Man 3: As man amongst men I'm a responsible man.
Man 4: As a man amongst men I'm a peaceful man
Man 5: As a man amongst men I'm a protecting man.
Craig: As a man amongst men I'm a worrier man
- Celebration-
00:26 Link: Bongani

Bongani: The night Craig Wilsons and his family became victim to a highjacking it changed his life forever. He decided to leave the big city and his high-powered corporate job to create social change in south Africa. This gave birth to his community based NGO – Father a Nation
00:44 Interview with Craig Craig: The whole idea behind Father a Nation is that if we could heal and restore men to be good fathers, good role models and good mentors we could absolute heal that community, and we could heal by extension of society and South Africa.
00:57 Group discussion And every one of us men there is still a little boy here, that little boy who wanted his dad to hold him and love him. Sometimes that boy is wounded, a wounded boy is the one fights, who drinks, who messes around
01:13 Link Bongani: In a country where 9 million children come from fatherless homes and that became the focus of Craig’s work.
01:19 Craig Craig: we became to realize as we interviewed schools, headmasters and headmistresses and NGO and government Department that the single biggest missing factor in families was the dad’s. So some dads were missing in action or present but not engage which is something that happened throughout society regardless of what LSM you belong to. Was I had a difficult childhood with regards to my father, I had a brother who committed suicide at the age of 20, and we had all kinds of difficult things. But when I had my children it was such an incredible revelation that they became the greatest inspiration I've ever had to get my life as a man right and if I look back in my life it could’ve gone horribly array if hadn’t been for them so seeing them and loving that made me very much into the person I am today.
02:04 Bongani link Bongani: Father a Nation is currently in De Aar holding its 3rd program for men. It’s a town where one of South Africa’s primary railway junctions but since the trains stop coming it has become a dusty place battles to find hope with 50% unemployment rate
02:23 Craig: Well the reason we came to De Aar was its got the worlds worse Fetal Alcohol syndrome; problem. People form America come to De Aar and all around the world to study fetal alcohol syndrome, that’s a very broken society
02:36 Bongani: Sam is one of the 50 men De Aar in the Father a Nation Program
02:43 My mother and father are alcoholics. They would fight and argue and break things. They would break cups and plates when they argued. That hurt me; I did not want my father to hit my mother. I was on my mother’s side but I was too young to defend her. So he would always overpower her. When I was growing up my father never told me he loved me or that I was safe. And he was never really around enough to tell me that. My father is dead now, I began drinking when I was 14, I started smoking dagga with the guys, and doing drugs with friends. I was trying to feel part of the group.
03:28 V/O about Francois Bongani: François Jonkers attended his first Father A Nation camp in De Aar 2016.
03:34 Francois interview Francois: My mother was a single parent; I grew up without my father. When I was 9 years he she died, I went to live with my grandmother and grandfather. When he was drink he always came in and started fighting and hitting my grandmother and hitting us. This is the stick he used to beat me; he’d sometimes beat me in my head with it. The bed would protect me so the he couldn’t continue to hit me. He would struggle to get me out from under the bed. What hurts me is to think in there times there was no-one who looked after me or someone to be there for me just to help me. I had a pencil, which I sharpened at both ends; it was my pencil that hots me through. If there was fighting in the house I would run to a piece of paper. That calmed me and at least helped me to get through the process.
04:47 Craig interview Craig: for a child the primary model is the same gender period. for a young boy growing up his primary role model is his dad and masculinity and how to be a man is imparted from a man to a boy and that very seldom happens in our society. Often men in the absence of a father they believe is that I wasn’t worse my dad sticking around for so the message he internalize I'm not worth and if I'm a broken man I'm going to be a broken father. And if I'm a wounded man chances are I'm going to wound my children.
05:17 Bongani: What happens later in life when children who come from fatherless homes well in South Africa the statistics are hard to come by but internationally studies have shown 75% of adolescents end up in rehab and 85% end up in jail.
05:37 Sam: The first time, in 2010, I got a 3-year jail sentence, that was case of attempted murder. I joined a gang – the 26’s. It wasn’t good to be in a gang because they stuff they did was not humane, it’s rough. When I came out of prison I had that prison mentality I makes me feel like I can do anything so I just started joining gangs and I wanted to be a leader. So when we come here and take told and pangas, garden forks and knives, we’d go to their den and start fighting. We caught one guy and stabbed him; we cut him with a panga across his head. The second time I spent 2 years and 6 months in jail. I think it was the stress that I grew up with; I actually blame my father for that.
06:38 Bongani: Alter his second stint in jail Sam was signed up by a local pastor to go on a father a Nation program. It starts with an intensive two-day camp followed by 12 weeks of counselling and planning for the future.
06:51 Men chanting * As a man amongst men you have hope*
06:58 Craig: so we take these men on a proudly healing journey. Men traditionally don't like to talk about their stuff do they? We don't like to admit that we cain’t. It’s a very intense 2-day 2-night process. Where there isn’t much sleep, not much food and there is a lot of deep processing just to get men to come to a place where they realize they would. Put them in circumstances where it came out and then bring the process of healing and restoration.
07:27 Sam: before the camp I had a reckless life, I didn’t care and I didn’t know about everything. So I used laugh at people who were sharing their stories then when it was my turn I was broken. The story of my father and I and how we were not good friends and that relationship – it broke me. That was the first time I had the opportunity to speak about what was in my heart and what bothered me inside.
07:59 Francois: I have made peace with what has happened in my life, and I've made peace with the circumstances regarding my grandmother. The problem didn’t rest with that time when I was growing up. The problem was from when he was a little child, now I understand he went through it and he didn’t want to deal with it
08:24 Sam: I can sat that before the camp I wasn’t good with my children, I didn’t spend quality time with them I was just that guy who came home and left. Not sit and chat with the family I didn’t do those things but now I do. I sit with people and watch TV, help my children with their homework. I am working through the things I have inside me day by day. I know I cain’t change overnight but u can try
08:57 Francois: before the camp I was actually passive in terms of what I should or wanted to do with my that held me back a lot. Now at the moment I work for myself, I am an artist. I am currently busy with painting murals of cartoons, the teachers and kids like it – they are blown away
09:22 Craig: the long term plan is to develop a network of men across all socio economic background to know what it mean to be a man, lets be a father to our children lets be husband to our wives, lets be mentors to our communities and just start that kind of movement to reach a critical mass where we begin to see serious impact on the nation.
09:40 Father a Nation Graduation Craig: we are here to celebrate the completion of a very exciting program. You went through a process where you were vulnerable, were you were strong, where you dealt with you own stuff inside

François: As a man I pledge
Sam: to use my strength well
Francois: to stand against any form of abuse
Sam: and to set an example to younger men
